title: Core Idea of Data Engineering
summary: Caching in data engineering is trading storage and staleness risk to avoid recomputing deterministic results. This concept page covers the mechanism, four patterns, honest trade-offs, production failures, and interview framing.

blocks.title: The one idea that matters
blocks.text: Caching does not make your pipeline faster. It lets you **skip work you already did**. Every cache design is a bet: **pay memory + staleness risk now to avoid compute + I/O later**. If you cannot name what work you are skipping, what key identifies it, and how you will know when the saved answer is wrong, you do not have a cache — you have a second source of truth waiting to diverge.
What it is, precisely

A cache in a data system is a **fast, lossy, time-bounded copy of a deterministic result**. Lossy means it can be dropped at any time without losing correctness, because the source of truth can recompute it. Time-bounded means every entry carries an explicit validity window — a TTL, a version, or an invalidation event — after which it must not be trusted. The result can be a row, a query response, a feature vector, an intermediate DataFrame partition, or a fully rendered dashboard tile. What matters is not the format, it is the contract: same key plus same source version must always produce the same bytes, or the cache will serve silently wrong answers.

Backend caching and data-engineering caching solve different pain. An API cache skips a 20 ms database round-trip to hit a 50 ms p99. A data cache skips a 40-minute aggregation, a full table scan over terabytes, or a feature join that costs real money on every training run. That changes the stakes. A 1% miss rate on an API cache is noise. A 1% miss rate on a cache shielding a warehouse means the warehouse still falls over at peak. **Trade-off:** the bigger the skipped work, the larger the payoff per hit — and the larger the blast radius when invalidation is late.
The mechanism

Every cache, from in-process `dict` to a distributed cluster to a materialized table used as a cache, runs the same loop: **key -> lookup -> hit or miss -> populate -> expire or invalidate**. The interview signal is whether you can draw the write path, not just the read path. Reads are easy. Writes decide whether readers see stale data for seconds, minutes, or forever. Name the key scheme, the hit path, the miss path, and the invalidation trigger before you argue about tools.

blocks.title: Cache read and write paths
blocks.caption: Hit path skips source. Miss path pays full cost once, then populates. Write path must invalidate or update.
blocks.code:
flowchart TD
  Q[Query or Pipeline Step] --> L{Cache Lookup by Key}
  L -->|Hit and TTL valid| H[Return Cached Bytes]
  L -->|Miss or Expired| S[Read Source of Truth]
  S --> C[Compute Serialize]
  C --> W[Write Cache with TTL or Version]
  W --> H
  U[Upstream Write or New Partition] --> V[Invalidate or Version-Bump Key]
  V --> L

blocks.text: On a hit you return bytes and touch recency metadata. On a miss you pay the full cost, then you populate the entry *with* its validity proof — TTL, source version, partition timestamp. The critical detail: **population must be atomic enough to avoid stampedes**. If 200 executors miss on `features/user_1234/date=2026-09-06` at once, naive code fires 200 warehouse queries. The fix is single-flight, request coalescing, or a short negative-cache lock: first misser computes, the rest wait on the same future. **Trade-off:** coalescing adds latency and coordination complexity to save downstream load — take it when the source is expensive and contended, skip it when the source is cheap.
Four patterns you must be able to draw

items: **Cache-aside / lazy load:** Reader checks cache, on miss reads source and writes back. Simple, best for read-heavy skewed workloads. Trade-off: first reader always pays, and you must handle stampedes yourself.

**Read-through / write-through:** Reader never touches source; cache library does. Writer writes to cache, cache writes to source synchronously. Stronger consistency, slower writes. Trade-off: you buy simpler app code with higher write latency and a cache on the critical write path.

**Write-behind / write-back:** Writer acks after cache write, cache flushes to source async. Lowest write latency, highest loss risk. Trade-off: you risk losing acknowledged writes on cache failure — unacceptable for billing or exactly-once pipelines unless you have a durable log in front.

**Materialized result as cache:** Precomputed table, aggregate rollup, or feature store offline table. Populated by scheduled pipeline, read by serving path. Trade-off: you get SQL-queryable, versioned caching with minutes-to-hours staleness instead of milliseconds — correct for analytics, fatal for auth checks.

blocks.text: Trade-offs, honestly

blocks.caption: No pattern wins. Each buys one property by selling another.
rows: Cache-aside with TTL
Simple to reason about, no coupling of write path, survives cache loss trivially
Stale reads until TTL expires; thundering herd on hot-key expiry unless you add jitter or single-flight
Read-through + write-through
App code stays dumb; read-your-write within one node; no stampede logic in app
Cache becomes single point of failure for writes; 2x write latency; harder to scale write throughput
Write-behind queue
Sub-millisecond ingest acks, absorbs bursty writes
Unacknowledged-to-source window where data loss or reordering is possible; needs replay and reconciliation
Larger cache / longer TTL
Higher hit ratio, lower source cost, smoother p99
More memory cost, longer staleness window, slower adaptation to distribution shift in features
Versioned keys instead of delete-invalidate
No race between delete and repopulate; old readers finish safely
Key explosion and storage overhead; need GC for orphaned versions; clients must resolve current version

blocks.text: The honest summary interviewers want: **hit ratio is not the goal, avoided source cost per dollar of cache is**. A 95% hit ratio that caches 10 ms queries is worse than a 60% hit ratio that caches 30-minute shuffles. Size and TTL by *cost-times-frequency*, not by request count. Hot, expensive, slowly-changing keys deserve memory. Cold, cheap, fast-changing keys do not, even if they are numerous.
How it fails in production

Caches do not fail by throwing errors. They fail by being **slowly wrong, suddenly hot, or invisibly empty**. Slowly wrong is stale features that degrade a model for three days before anyone checks distribution. Suddenly hot is synchronized TTL expiry that turns one expensive query into ten thousand at 00:00. Invisibly empty is a deploy that changes serialization and drops hit ratio from 85% to 0% with no error log — just a warehouse bill spike and p99 cliff. Design for observability first: hit ratio per key prefix, miss cost, age of served entry, and invalidation lag. Without those four, you are guessing.

blocks.caption: Failure -> symptom you would actually see on call.
rows: Stampede on expiry
Latency spike + source timeouts exactly at TTL boundary, repeated hourly
No jitter, no single-flight; hot key recomputed by hundreds of workers at once
Stale read
Dashboard disagrees with source query; model metrics drift down after upstream backfill
TTL-only invalidation with no version check against partition watermark
Poisoned entry
Same wrong answer for one key until manual flush; restarts do not help
Unbounded caching of errors or unvalidated upstream nulls; missing negative-cache TTL
Key cardinality explosion
Memory evictions climb, hit ratio falls as traffic grows
High-cardinality IDs or timestamps embedded in key without bucketing or hashing
Inconsistent invalidate
Reader A sees new value, reader B sees old for minutes
Delete-based invalidation racing with repopulate across replicas; no version fencing

blocks.text: Eviction and TTL are load-bearing

`LRU` keeps recently touched keys and is correct when access is skewed — 5% of keys serve 90% of reads. `LFU` keeps frequently touched keys and survives scans that would flush LRU. `FIFO` with TTL is correct for immutable partitioned data where newer is not hotter, just newer. Pick by access shape, not by default. For TTL, never use a single global value. Set `TTL < tolerable staleness` and add jitter of 10-20% to desynchronize expiry. **Trade-off:** per-key TTLs and version checks cost metadata lookups and code paths, but they are the only way to hold both a 24-hour dimension cache and a 30-second counter cache in one cluster without one poisoning the other.

blocks.code:
import time, hashlib
from threading import Lock

_store: dict[str, tuple[float, object]] = {}
_inflight: dict[str, Lock] = {}
_global_lock = Lock()

def _key(namespace: str, params: dict) -> str:
    # Stable, bounded-cardinality key: hash volatile parts, bucket time.
    raw = f"{namespace}:{sorted(params.items())}"
    return "v1:" + hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()[:32]

def get_or_compute(namespace, params, compute_fn, ttl_s=300):
    k = _key(namespace, params)
    now = time.time()
    ent = _store.get(k)
    if ent and ent[0] > now:
        return ent[1]  # hit
    # single-flight: only one worker recomputes per key
    with _global_lock:
        lock = _inflight.setdefault(k, Lock())
    with lock:
        ent = _store.get(k)  # recheck after acquiring
        if ent and ent[0] > time.time():
            return ent[1]
        try:
            val = compute_fn()  # expensive: warehouse / feature join
        except Exception:
            # short negative cache: do NOT cache failure for full TTL
            _store[k] = (time.time() + 5, None)
            raise
        # jitter prevents synchronized expiry stampede
        jitter = ttl_s * 0.15
        _store[k] = (time.time() + ttl_s + jitter, val)
        return val

blocks.text: This snippet carries three production lessons in 30 lines. First, the key is **hashed and version-prefixed** (`v1:`) so you can roll serialization without flushing the world. Second, the double-checked lock gives you single-flight without a distributed coordinator — enough for one process, and the pattern extends to a shared lock for many. Third, failures get a 5-second negative entry, not the full TTL. **Trade-off:** in-process maps are free and fast but do not share hits across workers; move this exact logic to a sidecar or cluster when miss cost times worker count exceeds network cost.
Sizing it without guessing

Size from the working set, not from total data. Estimate: `cache_bytes = hot_keys * avg_value_bytes * replication_factor * 1.3_headroom`. `hot_keys` is keys touched per TTL window, not total keys ever. If 200k feature rows of 2 KB are touched every 5 minutes with 3x replication, you need ~1.6 GB, not 200 GB for the full table. Then check source budget: `misses_per_sec * source_cost_per_miss < source_max_qps`. If 5% misses at 2000 reads per second means 100 warehouse queries per second and the warehouse allows 20, your TTL is too short or your key too fine-grained — roll up by minute, not by second. **Trade-off:** coarser keys raise hit ratio and lower cardinality but increase staleness and over-fetch; bucket time and round IDs deliberately.

items: Track **hit ratio per prefix**, not global — one cold prefix hides one melting hot prefix.
Track **served-entry age** (now minus source timestamp) — this is your true staleness SLO.
Track **miss cost**: p99 compute time and source errors during misses, not just miss count.
Alert on **invalidation lag**: time from upstream commit to cache version bump. If lag exceeds TTL, TTL is lying.
Load-test expiry: force-expire the top 10 keys and watch source. If it tips over, you need jitter plus single-flight before launch.

blocks.text: How it shows up in an interview

items.title: Name the skipped work and key
items.text: Say: reads are X per second, source cost is Y ms or dollars, key is `entity:version:bucket`. If you start with tool choice before this, you lose points.

items.title: State consistency requirement
items.text: Say what staleness you can tolerate in seconds and what happens on stale: annoyance, money loss, or model decay. This picks TTL vs versioned vs write-through.

items.title: Draw both paths
items.text: Draw hit, miss-populate with single-flight, and write-invalidate. Explicitly call out the race: delete vs repopulate, and how versioning fixes it.

items.title: Do the back-of-envelope
items.text: Compute working set bytes and miss QPS vs source limit. Show why TTL of 60s fails and 5 min with jitter passes. Numbers beat adjectives.

items.title: Close with failure and metric
items.text: Name one failure you accept — e.g., 30s stale on backfill — and the metric that proves it: served-entry age + invalidation lag. Interviewers hire for owned trade-offs.

blocks.text: Misconceptions that fail you

items: **"Cache improves consistency."** It never does. It only preserves or weakens what the source gives. Every cache adds a staleness window — name it.
**"Higher hit ratio is always better."** Not if you bought it with a 24-hour TTL on fast-changing data. Hit ratio without staleness bound is vanity.
**"We will just invalidate on write."** Deletes race with concurrent reads and repopulates across replicas. Use versioned keys or conditional writes unless you can prove delete ordering.
**"One TTL fits all."** Counters, dimensions, and model features change at different speeds. A single TTL either starves the source or serves stale dimensions.
**"Caching errors is fine."** Caching a transient 500 for 10 minutes turns a blip into an outage. Use 3-5 second negative caching or do not cache failures at all.
**"Materialized tables are not caches."** They are — a scheduled aggregate is a durable, queryable cache with hours of staleness. Treat its pipeline watermark as its TTL and monitor it the same way.

blocks.text: When to use it and when not to

blocks.caption: Use caching to skip repeated deterministic work, not to fix a broken source.
rows: Reads are skewed: small hot set, high repeat rate within TTL window
Reads are uniform one-offs: full scans, ad-hoc exploration — cache never hits
Compute is expensive: multi-way joins, shuffles, embeddings, rollups
Compute is cheap and source is fast: extra hop adds latency without savings
Source version or watermark is available to bound staleness
Correctness needs read-your-write across devices with no version channel
Miss cost is survivable: source handles miss QPS with headroom
Cache shields a source that cannot survive 1% misses — fix source capacity first
Entries are immutable per version: `partition_date`, `model_version` in key
Keys embed raw user input or unbounded timestamps with no bucketing

blocks.title: What to say in one sentence if asked
blocks.text: **Caching stores a versioned copy of an expensive deterministic result so repeat reads skip recompute, trading memory and bounded staleness for lower latency and source load.** Then add: key is X, TTL or version is Y because staleness Z is acceptable, and single-flight plus jitter protects the source on expiry.
